summary: This note is a Wikipedia-style article on Arecaceae, the palm family: a group of perennial monocot flowering plants in the order Arecales, with about 181 genera and roughly 2,600 species, mostly in tropical and subtropical climates. It covers morphology (solitary or clustered growth, large evergreen fronds, anomalous secondary growth, record-setting sizes), etymology, range and habitat, taxonomy into six subfamilies, fossil evolution, economic and cultural uses, symbolism, endangered species, pests, and non-palm plants called palms.
one_line: Overview of Arecaceae, the palm family of about 2,600 mostly tropical monocot species, covering biology, evolution, uses, symbolism and conservation.
key_facts: Arecaceae is a family of perennial flowering plants in the monocot order Arecales.
Currently 181 genera with around 2,600 species of Arecaceae are known, most restricted to tropical and subtropical climates.
Ceroxylon quindiuense, Colombia's national tree, is the tallest monocot in the world, reaching up to 60 metres tall.
The coco de mer (Lodoicea maldivica) has the largest seeds of any plant, weighing 15–30 kilograms each.
Raffia palms (Raphia spp.) have the largest leaves of any plant, up to 25 metres long.
The Corypha species have the largest inflorescence of any plant, up to 7.5 metres tall.
The northernmost native palm is Chamaerops humilis, which reaches 44°N latitude along the coast of Liguria, Italy.
Uhl and Dransfield's 1987 classification organizes palms into 6 subfamilies.
Subfamily Arecoideae is the largest subfamily, with 14 tribes and over 100 genera.
Nypoideae contains only one species, Nypa fruticans, whose fruit floats.
The Arecaceae were the first modern family of monocots to appear in the fossil record, around 80 million years ago.
The date palm was cultivated by Mesopotamians and other Middle Eastern peoples 5000 years or more ago.
The type member of Arecaceae is the areca palm (Areca catechu), whose areca nut is chewed with betel leaf.
The palm branch was a symbol of triumph and victory in classical antiquity.
In 2006, at least 100 palm species were considered endangered, and nine species had been reported as recently extinct.
The rarest palm known is Hyophorbe amaricaulis, with only one living individual, at the Botanic Gardens of Curepipe in Mauritius.
